relationship: Renewed command following wholehearted-obedience declaration
rationale: Moses and the elders command keeping all these commandments, following the declaration that the Lord commanded these ordinances and judgments for wholehearted performance.

relationship: Same-chapter stone-and-plaster instruction with specified destination
rationale: The command to erect and plaster great stones after crossing Jordan is repeated with Mount Ebal explicitly designated as their location.

relationship: Stone-inscription command and later narrated writing
rationale: Deuteronomy commands writing the law on stones after crossing; the actual Joshua continuation records writing Moses' law on stones before Israel, without repeating the plaster detail.

relationship: Ebal construction command and narrated altar location
rationale: The stones are to be set up upon Mount Ebal; Joshua's actual continuation locates his altar on Mount Ebal, retaining the different objects described in these units.

relationship: Parallel altar-stone restrictions
rationale: Both restrict working altar stones with a blade or iron; Exodus forbids hewn stones and states defilement, while Deuteronomy expressly says no iron shall be laid upon them.

relationship: No-iron altar command and explicitly Mosaic construction
rationale: Joshua describes an altar of whole stones untouched by iron and expressly invokes Moses' written command, corresponding to the altar restriction here.

relationship: Whole-stone altar and burnt offerings commanded and narrated
rationale: Both specify a whole-stone altar and whole burnt offerings; Joshua's account expressly relates its construction and offerings to Moses' law.

relationship: Related altar sacrifices with preserved offering names
rationale: Deuteronomy commands a sacrifice of deliverance with eating and rejoicing; Joshua records the altar's sacrifice of well-being, preserving the differing supplied offering descriptions and additional meal instructions.

relationship: Repeated law-inscription command and later written law
rationale: The requirement to write all the law plainly on stones corresponds to Joshua's statement that he wrote Moses' law upon stones before Israel.

relationship: Peoplehood declaration and divine choice
rationale: Both declare Israel a people belonging to the Lord this day; chapter26 explicitly calls them His chosen possession, while this verse calls for silence and hearing.

relationship: Hearing and doing in adjacent covenant declarations
rationale: Both combine hearing the Lord's voice with performing commandments, ordinances or judgments, with chapter26 additionally specifying wholeheartedness and choosing God as their God.

relationship: Same-chapter introductory command and specified ceremonial roles
rationale: The announcement that Moses commanded the people introduces the named tribal mountain assignments and the Levites' instruction to address Israel aloud.

relationship: Gerizim's blessing role specified by tribes
rationale: The earlier command assigns blessing to Mount Gerizim; this verse names the six tribes who are to stand there after crossing Jordan.

relationship: Mountain assignment and later gathered assembly
rationale: Joshua places half of the gathered Israel near Gerizim and half near Ebal, explicitly recalling Moses' command, without repeating this verse's individual tribal list.

relationship: Ebal's curse role specified by tribes
rationale: The earlier instruction assigns the curse to Mount Ebal; this verse gives the particular six tribes designated to stand there for that declaration.

relationship: Ebal assignment and later two-mountain arrangement
rationale: Joshua describes half of Israel near Ebal and half near Gerizim with the ark and officials, corresponding to the commanded arrangement without reproducing the tribal names.

relationship: Same-chapter Levite announcement and congregational response
rationale: The direction for Levites to address all Israel loudly is followed by the first spoken curse and the instruction for all the people to answer So be it.

relationship: Image-making prohibition pronounced as a curse
rationale: The curse upon making a graven or molten image corresponds to the prohibition on making idols or likenesses; Deuteronomy additionally specifies craftsmanship and secret placement.

relationship: Parallel restrictions on manufactured worship objects
rationale: Both prohibit manufactured images and describe prohibited placement; Leviticus names pillars and conspicuous stones for worship, while this curse names a secretly placed crafted image.

relationship: Curse for dishonour and positive parental command
rationale: The curse upon dishonouring father or mother is the negative counterpart of the command to honour both parents, where wellbeing and long land life accompany obedience.

relationship: Boundary-removal prohibition and corresponding curse
rationale: Both address removing a neighbour's boundaries; chapter19 identifies them as established in the allotted inheritance, while this verse pronounces the congregationally affirmed curse.

relationship: Related prohibitions on harming blind persons in their path
rationale: The curse forbids leading the blind astray on the road; Leviticus forbids putting a stumbling block before the blind, preserving the particular differing actions.

relationship: Repeated protection of the same three groups' judgment
rationale: Both forbid perverting the judgment of the sojourner, orphan and widow; chapter24 additionally prohibits taking the widow's garment in pledge.

relationship: Father's wife prohibition and paternal-covering explanation
rationale: Both prohibit the sexual act involving one's father's wife and explain its relation to the father's own covering or nakedness, preserving the supplied terms.

relationship: Parallel prohibition of sexual relations with animals
rationale: Both prohibit lying with an animal; Leviticus gives further male and female descriptions and defilement language, while Deuteronomy supplies the congregational curse.

relationship: Sister prohibition with paternal and maternal scope
rationale: Both specify the sister who is a daughter of the father or mother; Leviticus also distinguishes birth at home or outside.

relationship: Wife's-sister clause within the combined source unit
rationale: The second curse in this source unit concerns lying with the wife's sister; Leviticus prohibits taking a woman alongside her living sister, while the mother-in-law clause remains a separate first curse.

relationship: Treacherous attack and deceitful killing
rationale: The curse upon striking a neighbour treacherously corresponds to the law concerning attacking a neighbour to kill by deceit; Exodus additionally denies altar refuge in that case.

relationship: Innocent life and corrupt payment
rationale: The curse joins a bribe with killing an innocent person; Exodus prohibits killing the innocent and receiving gifts that corrupt judgment, without treating all its cases as one transaction.

relationship: Explicit citation of the law-observance curse
rationale: Galatians expressly cites the curse upon everyone who does not abide by all the written law to do it, using it in the argument about works of law.

relationship: Obedient chosen people placed above the nations
rationale: Both combine keeping the Lord's commandments with Israel's special standing above the nations; chapter26 calls them His possession and holy people, while chapter28 states the condition explicitly.

relationship: Blessing conditioned on hearing commandments
rationale: Both explicitly make blessing conditional upon hearkening to the Lord's instruction, with this verse introducing the blessings that will come upon the obedient people.

relationship: Same-chapter matched city-and-field blessing and curse
rationale: The blessing upon city and field is later reversed by a curse naming those exact two settings, retaining the deliberate positive and negative pairing.

relationship: Parallel human, agricultural and livestock fertility blessings
rationale: Both promise blessing on human offspring, land produce and livestock increase; chapter7 also explicitly names grain, wine and oil within that provision.

relationship: Same-chapter reversed blessing of offspring and produce
rationale: The later curse repeats this verse's human offspring, land produce, herds and flocks, reversing the blessing across the same enumerated areas.

relationship: Same-chapter storehouse-and-reserve blessing reversed
rationale: The same storehouses and reserves blessed here are explicitly cursed later, preserving the matched storage vocabulary rather than substituting a different edition's objects.

relationship: Same-chapter coming-and-going blessing reversed
rationale: Both mention coming in and going out, with the later curse reversing the blessing and the order of the two movements.

relationship: Related promises of enemy defeat and disproportionate pursuit
rationale: Both promise enemies falling before Israel and describe disproportionate flight or pursuit; Deuteronomy gives one approach and seven escape routes, while Leviticus gives different pursuer ratios.

relationship: Same-chapter exact reversal of one-way and seven-way warfare
rationale: Enemies coming by one way and fleeing by seven are reversed when Israel goes out one way and flees seven ways, changing which side suffers defeat.

relationship: Same-chapter opposed results upon the work of the hands
rationale: Blessing upon whatever Israel puts its hand to is reversed by want, famine and wasting upon whatever it undertakes after forsaking the Lord.

relationship: Holy peoplehood and keeping the chosen people's commands
rationale: Both describe Israel established or chosen as the Lord's holy people in connection with keeping His commandments, with the earlier passage also naming renown among nations.

relationship: Promised fear among the peoples
rationale: Both promise that other peoples will fear Israel through the Lord's action; this verse specifically connects their response with seeing His name called upon Israel.

relationship: Repeated multiplication across womb, field and livestock
rationale: Both connect the land sworn to the fathers with blessing or multiplication in human offspring, field produce and livestock offspring, preserving the specific threefold provision.

relationship: Seasonal heavenly rain and fruitful work
rationale: Both promise rain in its season for the land; chapter11 specifies early and latter rain and named crops, while this verse also speaks of the heavenly treasury and blessed work.

relationship: Repeated international lending and rule promise
rationale: Both state that Israel will lend to many nations without borrowing and rule without being ruled, with this verse additionally giving rain and work as blessings.

relationship: Same-chapter head-and-tail positions reversed
rationale: The promise that Israel will be head rather than tail is reversed when the sojourner becomes lender and head while Israel becomes tail.

relationship: Repeated prohibition of turning right or left
rationale: Both forbid turning from the commanded words to right or left; this verse specifically identifies following and serving other gods as the deviation in view.

relationship: Disobedience condition introducing covenant judgments
rationale: Both introduce adverse covenant consequences through failure to obey and perform the Lord's commands; Leviticus additionally names dissolving the covenant before beginning its particular afflictions.

relationship: Same-chapter city-and-field curse reversing blessing
rationale: The city and field cursed here are the exact two settings blessed at the start of the chapter, giving a particular matched reversal.

relationship: Same-chapter curse upon the previously blessed stores
rationale: The curse repeats the storehouses and reserves of the earlier blessing, reversing its outcome for those same named provisions.

relationship: Same-chapter offspring-and-produce curse reversing the same list
rationale: Human offspring, land produce, cattle herds and sheep flocks recur from the blessing list, now explicitly under the opposite pronouncement.

relationship: Same-chapter daily-movement curse reversing blessing
rationale: Going out and coming in receive the curse instead of the earlier blessing upon coming in and going out, preserving both movements and the changed order.

relationship: Same-chapter frustrated work contrasting with blessed work
rationale: Want, famine and wasting strike whatever the hand undertakes after forsaking the Lord, reversing the earlier promise of blessing upon those same undertakings.

relationship: Death included among covenant afflictions
rationale: Both announce death coming upon the people within covenant judgment; Leviticus places it amid sword, city flight and enemy delivery, while Deuteronomy says it cleaves until land removal.

relationship: Related illness-and-wasting judgment lists with distinct terms
rationale: Both list bodily afflictions within covenant warnings, but the particular fevers, chills, inflammation and other terms here differ from Leviticus' distress, scab and jaundice.

relationship: Metal heaven-and-earth images with exchanged assignments
rationale: Both describe heaven and earth with iron and bronze under judgment; Deuteronomy assigns bronze to heaven and iron to earth, while Leviticus reverses those assignments.

relationship: Rain withheld in threatened land judgment
rationale: The dust replacing rain develops the earlier warning that the Lord will shut heaven so rain and fruit fail, while retaining the distinct imagery in each passage.

relationship: Same-chapter reversal of the identical battlefield route pattern
rationale: Israel's one-way advance and seven-way flight reverse the earlier promise that its enemies would approach one way and flee seven ways.

relationship: Parallel warnings of defeat and flight before enemies
rationale: Both describe Israel falling before enemies and fleeing; Leviticus adds flight when no one pursues, while Deuteronomy gives the one-and-seven pattern and scattering among kingdoms.

relationship: Closely repeated unguarded-corpse judgment
rationale: Both describe the people's dead becoming food for heaven's birds and earth's beasts, with no one to drive the creatures away.

relationship: Same-chapter incurable ulcer descriptions with different locations
rationale: Both threaten grievous ulceration that cannot be healed; this verse mentions the Egyptian ulcer upon the buttocks, while the later verse names knees, legs and the whole body.

relationship: Same-chapter blindness threat and described groping
rationale: The threat of blindness and mental bewilderment is followed by the particular image of groping at noon as the blind grope in darkness.

relationship: Shared blindness, groping and noonday-darkness imagery
rationale: Both describe blind-like groping and noon becoming like darkness or midnight; Isaiah places the image within the community's confession of absent judgment and salvation.

relationship: House, vineyard and wife losses across distinct settings
rationale: Both enumerate a house, vineyard and wife that another may possess or enjoy; the war exemptions seek to avert such loss, while this curse announces it.

relationship: Same-chapter livestock loss and the invading consumer
rationale: The calf, donkey and sheep losses anticipate the later invader consuming livestock offspring and leaving no cattle or sheep, preserving the distinct animals and actions in each description.

relationship: Same-chapter children transferred to another nation and captivity
rationale: Sons and daughters given to another nation correspond to the later explanation that children will not remain with their parents because they go into captivity.

relationship: Parallel loss of agricultural labour to enemies
rationale: Both describe the people's sown produce being consumed by adversaries or an unknown nation, turning their cultivation and labour into provision for others.

relationship: Same-chapter madness provoked by specified witnessed losses
rationale: Madness from what the eyes see follows cattle seized or slaughtered, children taken away and foreigners consuming the land's yield, specifying the distressing sights in this sequence.

relationship: Same-chapter incurable affliction revisited over different body regions
rationale: The unhealable ulcer upon knees, legs and from foot to crown corresponds to the earlier incurable Egyptian ulcer and skin afflictions, while the described locations remain distinct.

relationship: Scattering and service to wooden and stone gods
rationale: Both warn of being taken among other nations and serving gods of wood and stone; this verse expressly includes the people and the rulers they appoint.

relationship: National suffering made a subject of outsiders' speech
rationale: The warning that Israel becomes a riddle, parable and tale among nations corresponds to the later scene of descendants and foreigners observing the devastated land and asking why.

relationship: Sowing without benefiting from the harvest
rationale: Both announce sowing without the expected harvest; Deuteronomy specifies much seed, little gathered and locust consumption, while Micah's shorter statement gives no locust cause.

relationship: Wine production without drinking its result
rationale: Both deny the producer the enjoyment of wine; Deuteronomy names planted and dressed vineyards lost to worms, while Micah describes wine pressed but not drunk.

relationship: Olive labour without anointing oil
rationale: Both explicitly describe failure to anoint oneself with oil despite olive provision or labour; Deuteronomy names falling olives and Micah speaks of pressing them.

relationship: Same-chapter captivity explaining loss of children
rationale: Children born but not retained because of captivity correspond to the earlier statement that sons and daughters are given to another nation before their powerless parents.

relationship: Parallel failure of trees and field produce
rationale: Both announce loss of the land's agricultural yield and trees' fruit; Deuteronomy attributes the consumption to blight, while Leviticus states that field and tree will not yield.

relationship: Same-chapter reversal of relative height and standing
rationale: The sojourner rising higher as Israel descends reverses the promised position of Israel above rather than beneath, with the following verse specifying the lender-and-borrower relationship.

relationship: Lending and rule blessing reversed in the sojourner relation
rationale: The earlier promise makes Israel lender rather than borrower and ruler rather than ruled; here the sojourner lends while Israel does not, becoming head while Israel is tail.

relationship: Same-chapter announced curse condition restated as a closing summary
rationale: The summary repeats the opening threat of curses coming upon and overtaking those who fail to hear and keep the commands, now adding pursuit and destruction.

relationship: Afflictions as signs for descendants and outside observers
rationale: The curses become signs upon the people and their seed; the later scene describes coming descendants and foreigners observing land-plagues and asking the meaning of that anger.

relationship: Failure of glad service contrasted with commanded rejoicing
rationale: The charge of failing to serve gladly amid abundance contrasts with the command to eat before the Lord and rejoice with the household because of His blessing.

relationship: Enemy servitude and an iron collar reversing liberation imagery
rationale: The curse places an iron collar upon Israel in enemy service; Leviticus recalls release from Egyptian slavery through a shattered yoke, preserving their distinct bondage imagery.

relationship: Same-chapter two contrasting forms of service
rationale: Failure to serve the Lord gladly amid abundance is followed by compelled enemy service amid hunger, thirst, nakedness and lack, making the contrast explicit.

relationship: Distant invading nation with unintelligible speech
rationale: Both announce a nation brought from far away whose speech Israel will not understand; Deuteronomy additionally compares its coming with an eagle's swoop.

relationship: Merciless invader description and later invasion narrative
rationale: Deuteronomy describes disregard for aged and young; Chronicles recounts young men killed, virgins unspared and elders carried away, retaining the different fates without asserting an exclusive fulfillment.

relationship: Invader consuming harvest and livestock
rationale: Both describe the invading nation's consumption of agricultural produce and livestock, with Jeremiah naming vineyards, figs and olives and Deuteronomy naming grain, wine, oil, cattle and sheep.

relationship: Destruction of trusted fortified cities
rationale: Both explicitly describe the attacking nation destroying fortified cities in which the people trusted; Deuteronomy expands this into siege throughout the cities and collapsing high walls.

relationship: Parallel threat of eating sons' and daughters' flesh
rationale: Both explicitly threaten eating the flesh of one's own sons and daughters; Deuteronomy additionally states the besieging enemy and desperate distress as the circumstances.

relationship: Same-chapter delicate man's hostility and the withheld food
rationale: The delicate man's grudging attitude toward brother, wife and remaining children is explained by the next verse as withholding the flesh he eats when nothing else remains.

relationship: Child-flesh threat developed through siege scarcity
rationale: The man's secretive withholding of children's flesh develops the same threatened eating of sons and daughters stated concisely in Leviticus, adding the siege and lack of other food.

relationship: Same-chapter delicate woman's hostility and desperate consumption
rationale: The woman's extreme delicacy and grudging attitude to husband and children are followed by the stated secret consumption of afterbirth and her child amid siege deprivation.

relationship: Same-chapter particular maternal case within the siege warning
rationale: The detailed case of afterbirth and a newborn consumed secretly elaborates the earlier general warning that parents will eat their children under an enemy's desperate siege.

relationship: Same-chapter written-law and divine-name condition followed by plagues
rationale: Failure to perform the written law and fear the honoured divine name introduces the next verse's extraordinary, enduring afflictions upon the people and their offspring.

relationship: Same-chapter enduring disease announcement expanded by scope
rationale: The great, enduring plagues upon parents and offspring are developed by the following references to dreaded Egyptian sufferings and infirmities not written in the law book.

relationship: Egyptian disease promise reversed
rationale: The earlier obedient blessing withholds the grievous diseases of Egypt from Israel; this curse instead brings back the dreaded Egyptian sufferings to cleave to them.

relationship: Same-chapter written law and extension to unlisted plagues
rationale: The condition concerns doing the written law and is followed by announced diseases; verse61 extends the threatened infirmities beyond those written in that book.

relationship: Star-like multiplication reversed into diminished numbers
rationale: The earlier recital celebrates growth from the Egyptian household into a star-like multitude; this curse explicitly contrasts that same star-like former multitude with being left few.

relationship: Repeated warning of reduced numbers among nations
rationale: Both announce that Israel will be left few, with chapter4 explicitly placing this within scattering among nations and chapter28 naming failure to heed the Lord.

relationship: Divine rejoicing over prosperity reversed and later renewed
rationale: The curse contrasts former rejoicing in good and multiplication with removal and destruction; the restoration promise says the Lord will again rejoice over the people for good.

relationship: Repeated dispersion and wooden-and-stone-god service
rationale: Both describe scattering among nations and service to other gods made of wood and stone; chapter4 additionally emphasizes those gods' inability to perceive or act.

relationship: Fear and wasting in the enemies' land
rationale: Both describe faintheartedness, fear and wasting amid foreign peoples or enemies' lands; Leviticus adds terror at a windborne leaf and flight without a pursuer.

relationship: Same-chapter day-and-night insecurity and its voiced longing
rationale: The threatened lack of assurance for life by day and night is developed through wishing each morning for evening and each evening for morning because of fear.

relationship: Same-chapter alternating wishes express continual fear
rationale: The morning-and-evening wishes express the preceding threat that life will lack assurance and the people will fear continually by day and night.

relationship: Egyptian return contrary to the no-return declaration
rationale: Both recall the declaration against returning by the Egyptian way; chapter17 applies it to a ruler's horse policy, while this curse threatens return by ships and enslavement.

relationship: Moab covenant heading distinguished from Horeb covenant
rationale: This heading explicitly places the commanded covenant in Moab besides the Horeb covenant; chapter5 recalls the Horeb covenant and addresses its living hearers, without merging the occasions.

relationship: Egyptian deeds before the addressed eyewitnesses
rationale: Both recall the Lord's deeds against Pharaoh and Egypt before the hearers; chapter11 additionally specifies the pursuing army and the sea's destruction.

relationship: Repeated eyewitness description of trials, signs and wonders
rationale: Both use great trials, signs and wonders seen by the people's eyes to characterize the Egyptian deliverance, with chapter7 applying their memory against fear of other nations.

relationship: Same-chapter witnessed signs contrasted with ungranted understanding
rationale: The statement about not yet receiving heart, eyes and ears to know follows the assertion that the hearers saw the Egyptian signs, preserving the text's deliberate contrast.

relationship: Forty-year garment preservation with distinct foot descriptions
rationale: Both describe garments preserved during forty wilderness years; this verse says sandals did not wear away, while chapter8 says the feet did not become calloused.

relationship: Wilderness food and learning dependence upon God
rationale: The absence of ordinary bread, wine and strong drink is stated as a means to know the Lord; chapter8 describes unfamiliar manna and learning that life depends on God's word.

relationship: Sihon's battle and defeat recalled
rationale: Both identify Sihon of Heshbon coming to battle and being struck; chapter2 additionally locates the engagement at Jahaz and attributes delivery to the Lord.

relationship: Og's battle and defeat recalled
rationale: Both name Og of Bashan as an opponent defeated by Israel; chapter3 supplies Edrei, the divine assurance and the defeat of his people.

relationship: Eastern lands assigned to the same tribes
rationale: Both assign the conquered land to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh; chapter3 gives the particular Gilead, Bashan and Argob distributions.

relationship: Careful law performance linked with understanding
rationale: Both connect keeping and doing the law's words with understanding one's actions; Joshua additionally instructs continual speech and day-and-night meditation upon the law book.

relationship: Same-chapter assembly list extended and its covenant purpose
rationale: The chiefs, elders, judges, officers and men standing before the Lord are joined by wives, children and sojourners, with the stated purpose of entering the covenant and curses.

relationship: Whole-community participation including children and resident aliens
rationale: Both expressly include women or wives, children and resident aliens in the gathered community; Joshua describes the assembly hearing every commanded word rather than this covenant-entry declaration.

relationship: Covenant entry follows the Moab covenant heading
rationale: The gathered people enter the Lord's covenant and curses after the heading identifying the commanded Moab covenant as additional to the Horeb covenant.

relationship: Reciprocal divine and communal covenant belonging
rationale: Both identify the Lord as Israel's God and Israel as His chosen people; this verse explicitly connects that establishment with the oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

relationship: Same-chapter covenant scope beyond the immediate hearers
rationale: The declaration that the covenant and curse concern more than the addressed group is completed by including both those present and those not present this day.

relationship: Different stated descriptions of covenant hearers
rationale: Chapter29 includes those present and absent, while chapter5 stresses the living hearers rather than their fathers; the comparison preserves both formulations without identifying every absent party.

relationship: Same-chapter travelled nations and observed idolatrous danger
rationale: The reminder of Egyptian residence and travel among nations leads into observed idols and the question whether anyone's mind has turned toward serving those nations' gods.

relationship: Manufactured idols described by their materials
rationale: Both describe gods or idols of wood and stone; chapter29 additionally names silver and gold, while chapter4 states the wooden and stone gods' inability to perceive.

relationship: Root-of-bitterness image reused in communal warning
rationale: Deuteronomy warns of a root springing up in gall and bitterness among potential idolaters; Hebrews uses a growing root of bitterness to warn of trouble and widespread defilement.

relationship: Potential other-god defection within intimate community
rationale: Both address enticement or turning toward other gods within families and the community; chapter13 gives the particular private-enticer case and commands refusing consent.

relationship: Same-chapter false self-blessing answered by rejected mercy
rationale: The person who pronounces wellbeing upon himself while following his wandering heart is answered by the declaration that God will not grant him mercy and covenant curses will cleave.

relationship: Same-chapter threatened individual judgment answers false assurance
rationale: The singular man's threatened erasure and covenant curses answer his preceding self-pronounced blessing, preserving the distinction between his private assurance and the announced response.

relationship: Same-chapter particular offender singled out within Israel
rationale: The statement that the Lord sets him apart from Israel for evils develops the preceding singular offender's curse and erased name, retaining the individual scope within the communal covenant.

relationship: Same-chapter coming observers and their question about the land
rationale: Future descendants and a distant foreigner observe the land's plagues; the following description specifies burned, barren ground and the nations' question about the Lord's anger.

relationship: Named Sodom-and-Gomorrah overthrow and sulfur judgment
rationale: The comparison explicitly names Sodom and Gomorrah; Genesis describes sulfur and fire overthrowing those cities and surrounding growth, while Deuteronomy also names Admah and Zeboiim and describes salt.

relationship: Same-chapter nations' question and stated covenant explanation
rationale: The question why the Lord treated the land this way receives the explicit answer of forsaking His covenant, serving other gods and bringing the written curses upon the land.

relationship: Same-chapter covenant abandonment specified as other-god worship
rationale: The declaration that the people forsook their fathers' covenant is immediately developed by their serving and bowing to other gods they did not know.

relationship: Foreign-god service linked with foreign-land servitude
rationale: Deuteronomy places other-god service before expulsion from the land; Jeremiah explicitly answers a similar why-question by connecting foreign-god worship at home with serving foreigners abroad.

relationship: Written covenant-curse explanation recalls its earlier announcement
rationale: The explanation that the Lord brings this book's curses upon the land corresponds to the earlier announcement that disobedience will cause all these curses to overtake Israel.

relationship: Parallel threatened removal and scattering from the land
rationale: Both describe divine removal or scattering of Israel among foreign lands; Leviticus additionally specifies desolate cities and an advancing sword, while Deuteronomy names wrath and indignation.

relationship: Revealed obligation and nearby performable instruction
rationale: The revealed things belong to the people for doing the law; the following chapter describes the command as accessible and the word near enough to perform, without claiming disclosure of hidden things.

relationship: Return considered within the earlier dispersion warning
rationale: Both describe Israel among nations after judgment and a subsequent return toward the Lord; chapter30 expressly calls the blessing and curse to the dispersed people's heart.

relationship: Blessing-and-curse pair recalled at the return instruction
rationale: The blessing and curse brought to mind among the nations recall the earlier explicit pairing, where hearing instruction brings blessing and deviation toward other gods brings curse.

relationship: Wholehearted turning and renewed hearing in dispersion
rationale: Both describe wholehearted seeking or return to the Lord and hearing His voice after distress or dispersion, retaining the distinct seek-and-find and return-and-obey formulations.

relationship: Mercy following the people's return
rationale: The promise of mercy and gathering develops the earlier assurance that the merciful Lord will not forsake the people or forget the fathers' covenant after their return.

relationship: Gathering reverses widely extended dispersion
rationale: The threat scatters Israel from end to end of earth, while the restoration promise gathers even from heaven's farthest extent; their different extent descriptions remain intact.

relationship: Restored ancestral land and remembered patriarchal covenant
rationale: Deuteronomy promises renewed inheritance of the fathers' land; Leviticus declares remembrance of the covenants of Jacob, Isaac and Abraham together with the land, without detailing the same return sequence.

relationship: Related heart transformation with distinct wording and agency
rationale: Chapter10 commands the people to circumcise heart-hardness; chapter30 promises that the Lord will thoroughly cleanse their hearts for wholehearted love and life, preserving both wording and agency.

relationship: Related redirection of affliction toward Israel's haters
rationale: Both describe affliction laid upon those who hate Israel; chapter7 specifies Egyptian diseases withheld from obedient Israel, while chapter30 transfers the curses within the restoration setting.

relationship: Same-chapter return and obedient hearing repeated
rationale: Both describe returning and obeying the Lord's voice and commandments, with verse2 explicitly naming wholeheartedness and verse8 restating performance of what Moses commands.

relationship: Repeated human, field and cattle provision
rationale: Both promise divine good in human offspring, land produce and cattle offspring, while chapter30 additionally describes renewed rejoicing over the people after return.

relationship: Renewed divine rejoicing reverses threatened loss
rationale: Chapter28 contrasts rejoicing to prosper with rejoicing to destroy and remove; chapter30 explicitly promises that the Lord will again rejoice over the people for good.

relationship: Same-chapter wholehearted return and commanded obedience reiterated
rationale: Both combine returning with all heart and soul and obeying the Lord's commands; verse10 expressly identifies the commands, ordinances and judgments as written in this law book.

relationship: Same-chapter accessible-command assertion and explanatory contrasts
rationale: The assertion that the command is neither excessively burdensome nor far away is explained through denied heavenly or sea journeys and the word's nearness for performance.

relationship: Heavenly-ascent question reused with Christ interpretation
rationale: Romans repeats the question of who will ascend into heaven and interprets it as bringing Christ down; Deuteronomy asks about fetching the command so it can be heard and done.

relationship: Same-chapter parallel rejected journeys to obtain instruction
rationale: The proposed sea crossing parallels the heavenly ascent question, each denied as a necessary means of fetching instruction for the people to hear and do.

relationship: Near-word statement reused with stated interpretive difference
rationale: Romans cites the word near in mouth and heart and calls it the proclaimed word of faith; Deuteronomy also includes hands and expressly relates the nearness to doing it.

relationship: Same-chapter life-and-death alternatives restated in the witness appeal
rationale: The life-and-death alternatives set before Israel are repeated when heaven and earth are invoked, now accompanied by the explicit appeal to choose life for descendants as well.

relationship: Love, walking, observance and wellbeing in covenant exhortation
rationale: Both combine loving the Lord, walking in His ways and keeping His commands or ordinances for Israel's good; this verse expressly adds multiplication and blessing in the inherited land.

relationship: Other-god turning and service in the warning condition
rationale: Both warn of turning from the Lord toward serving and bowing to other gods, with chapter8 explicitly adding forgetting and the witness against resulting destruction.

relationship: Repeated threatened perishing instead of long land life
rationale: Both declare perishing and denial of prolonged days upon the land entered across Jordan, retaining the specific contrast between inherited land and shortened tenure.

relationship: Heaven and earth invoked as witnesses concerning land life
rationale: Both call heaven and earth as witnesses concerning Israel's future in the land; chapter30 couples the appeal with choosing life, while chapter4 announces perishing under idolatry.

relationship: Love, cleaving and lengthened life in the sworn land
rationale: Both connect loving and cleaving to the Lord with prolonged days upon the land sworn to the fathers; chapter11 additionally names sons and walking in His ways.
